nameStory: Big bluestem gets its name from its impressive height and the distinctive blue-purple tinge that colors its stems, especially at the base and joints. The 'big' part distinguishes it from its shorter cousin, little bluestem, making it the giant of the bluestem family.
description: Big bluestem is a magnificent tall prairie grass that can tower over your head, reaching 4-8 feet in height. This native grass forms dense clumps with long, narrow leaves that cascade gracefully from sturdy blue-tinged stems. In late summer, it produces distinctive three-pronged seed heads that look remarkably like turkey feet, earning it the nickname 'turkeyfoot.' It's a warm-season grass, meaning it does most of its growing during the hot summer months.

idTips.label: Seed Heads
idTips.description: The unmistakable three-pronged seed clusters look exactly like turkey feet, with each 'toe' being 2-4 inches long and purplish-bronze in color

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Sturdy stems show a beautiful blue to purple tinge, especially noticeable at the joints and base - run your finger along them to feel their smooth, solid texture

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Long, narrow leaves (about 1/4 to 1/2 inch wide) feel rough to the touch and may have a slight fold down the middle, with edges that can be sharp enough to cause paper cuts

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense, upright clumps that can reach 4-8 feet tall, creating an impressive fountain-like appearance that sways gracefully in the wind

idTips.label: Winter Appearance
idTips.description: Persists through winter as golden-tan clumps with the distinctive three-pronged seed heads still visible, creating beautiful winter interest

habitat: In New England, big bluestem thrives in open, sunny areas with well-drained soils, particularly in restored prairies, old fields, and grassland preserves. You'll often find it in conservation areas and along roadsides where prairie restoration efforts have been undertaken. It prefers full sun and can tolerate drought once established, making it popular in native plant gardens and naturalized landscapes.

seasonality.spring: New green shoots emerge late in spring, much later than cool-season grasses, starting as small tufts at the base of old clumps.
seasonality.summer: Rapid growth occurs during hot weather, with stems elongating and the characteristic blue coloring becoming more pronounced at the joints.
seasonality.fall: The spectacular turkey-foot seed heads appear in late summer through fall, turning from purplish to golden-bronze as they mature and catch the autumn light beautifully.
seasonality.winter: Dried golden clumps persist through winter, with seed heads still attached, providing food for birds and striking architectural form in the snowy landscape.

funFact: Big bluestem's roots can plunge an incredible 15 feet deep into the soil - that's deeper than most trees! This amazing root system allowed it to survive prairie fires and drought, and it's why prairie soils became some of the richest farmland in North America.
confusionNotes: Big bluestem is most easily confused with little bluestem, but little bluestem is much shorter (2-4 feet), has fluffy white seed heads instead of turkey feet, and turns brilliant orange-red in fall. Remember: big bluestem = big turkey feet, little bluestem = little white fluff.
contextualKnowledge: Though big bluestem is native to eastern North America including parts of New England, it was much more abundant before European settlement. Most of New England's natural grasslands were converted to agriculture or developed, so today you'll mainly see big bluestem in restoration projects and native plant gardens rather than wild prairie remnants.
compareHints: Big bluestem is the only bluestem species commonly found in New England, making identification easier. When compared to other tall grasses in the region like switchgrass or reed grass, big bluestem's turkey-foot seed heads are completely unique - no other grass produces that distinctive three-pronged pattern. The blue-purple stem coloring also sets it apart from most other native grasses.
